Microsoft AI Buyouts


# Microsoft Offers Buyouts to 60,000 Employees as Nadella Says AI Is Why


By OpenTools Team


·


November 21, 2026


Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees — 27% of its workforce — as CEO Satya Nadella says AI is fundamentally reshaping roles. The program lets employees choose whether to be part of the AI transition or leave. Builders should watch what happens when the world's largest software company retools around AI.


## 60,000 Offers, One Reason: AI


[Microsoft](https://opentools.ai/organizations/microsoft) has offered voluntary buyouts to approximately **60,000 employees** — roughly 27% of its global workforce of about 223,000 — with CEO Satya Nadella drawing a direct line between the program and the company's AI transformation,[Crypto Briefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/microsoft-nadella-ai-buyouts-60000-employees/) reported.


The program, which began in October, is open to vice president-level employees and below in the US, Canada, UK, and India. US employees who accept get at least 8 weeks of base pay plus transition support. The opt-in deadline is early December, with departures effective December 31.


Speaking at the New York Times Dealbook Summit on November 18, Nadella framed the buyouts as giving employees choice at a moment of profound change. Rather than simply laying off workers, he said the program was designed to give employees some measure of control over their future,[Computerworld](https://www.computerworld.com/article/4251449/nadella-heres-why-microsoft-offered-buyouts-to-60000-employees.html) reported.


## From Layoffs to Buyouts: Microsoft's AI Retooling


The buyout program follows years of workforce reductions at[Microsoft](https://opentools.ai/organizations/microsoft) : roughly 10,000 jobs cut in 2023, more than 15,000 in 2025, and another 4,800 earlier in 2026. Expected uptake for this round is below 5% — fewer than 3,000 employees — making it a modest trim compared to past mass layoffs.


But the shift from involuntary layoffs to voluntary buyouts is significant. It signals that Microsoft is not simply cutting costs — it is **actively reshaping its workforce around AI** . Nadella pointed to a specific example: a development team working on Copilot in Microsoft 365 that consists of just 11 people. They are not building the product themselves, he said — they are building a software factory that builds the product,[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-why-he-asked-60k-employees-to-quit/) reported.


That distinction — managing AI agents rather than doing the work directly — is the core of Nadella's pitch. His message to employees: you will manage AI, not be replaced by it. But offering 27% of the company an exit suggests the transition will be anything but smooth.


## The $175 Billion Bet Behind the Buyouts


[Microsoft](https://opentools.ai/organizations/microsoft) 's AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach **$175 billion in 2026** , according to Crypto Briefing. The buyouts are one piece of a much larger reallocation: capital and headcount are moving from traditional software roles toward AI infrastructure and agent-based development.


For developers and builders, this is the most important signal in the announcement. When the world's largest software company says an 11-person team can manage what used to require hundreds, the economics of software development are fundamentally changing. **AI agents are becoming the primary workforce** , and the remaining humans are becoming managers and architects of agent systems.


## What This Means for the Broader Tech Workforce


[Microsoft](https://opentools.ai/organizations/microsoft) is not alone. The tech industry has seen roughly 175,000 layoffs in 2026 so far, with AI increasingly cited as the direct cause. Salesforce initiated another round of cuts this week, while Ubisoft eliminated 166 jobs as it builds an[AI studio](https://opentools.ai/tools/ai-studio) . The pattern is consistent: companies are reducing traditional roles while investing heavily in AI infrastructure.


Nadella's buyout approach may become a template. Voluntary exits carry less reputational risk than mass layoffs and let companies target specific demographics — but they also carry selection risk. The employees most likely to accept buyouts are often the ones with the most options elsewhere. If a larger-than-expected share of top engineers takes the offer, Microsoft could lose exactly the talent it needs for the AI transition.


For builders, the signal is clear: the era of AI workforce restructuring is accelerating. Companies are not waiting for gradual adoption — they are actively reshaping their org charts around agent-based workflows. The skills that remain valuable are architecture, orchestration, and agent management, not line-by-line implementation.


## What to Watch


Three things to track in the coming weeks:


- **Uptake rate.** If acceptance exceeds the expected 5%, it signals that employee anxiety about AI is higher than[Microsoft](https://opentools.ai/organizations/microsoft) anticipated. If it is lower, the workforce may be betting that the transition creates more opportunity than risk.
- **Which roles leave.** The most important signal is not how many leave, but which functions see the highest exit rates. If[AI research](https://opentools.ai/tools/ai-research) and engineering teams stay while support and operations depart, the AI bet is working as designed.
- **Competitor responses.** If[Google](https://opentools.ai/organizations/google) , Meta, and Amazon follow with similar voluntary programs, the buyout template becomes the new standard for AI-driven workforce restructuring across Big Tech.
